title: {{NAME}} and the Unicorn Who Played in Goal
moral: The most magical things often come to you when you stop looking and just play.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a turquoise soccer jersey with a silver star, white shorts, and turquoise cleats — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} was practising penalty kicks alone in the park when the unicorn walked onto the pitch.

She stood in the goal and looked at him.

Her horn was the colour of starlight and her coat was white-silver and her eyes were the patient expression of someone who had been waiting for a while.

{{NAME}} looked at her. Looked at his ball. Looked back at her.

"Are you going to move?" he asked.

She did not move.

"Right," said {{NAME}}. "Let's see it then."

pages.content:
She was extraordinary in goal.

Not because she was fast or could dive: she was neither fast nor a diver. She simply stood wherever the ball was going to be before it went there.

Penalty after penalty hit her side, her flank, her nose (once). She absorbed them all with serene indifference.

{{NAME}} stopped after the twentieth kick.

"How do you do that?" he asked.

She touched the ground with one hoof, marking a spot. Then she tapped his boot.

He looked at the spot she'd touched. It was exactly where he'd been aiming without realising it.

pages.content:
She was teaching him, he realised.

Every practice session, she stood in goal and showed him not what he thought he was doing, but what he was actually doing: the unconscious lean, the shoulder that telegraphed direction, the foot angle that was invisible to him but obvious to her.

He started changing things. Hid his weight. Changed his run-up. Learned to shoot before his body had committed to a direction.

After three weeks, he put one past her.

Just one. But her ears went up and she made a sound he'd never heard her make before: something very like pride.

pages.content:
He brought his teammates to practice with her.

Not one of them scored for two full sessions. Then, one by one, as she showed each of them their own unconscious tells, they began to figure it out.

By the end of the month, his team had the best penalty record in the local league.

"We have a secret weapon," his teammate Kiri said.

"She's not a weapon," said {{NAME}}. "She's a teacher."

The unicorn, from the goal, inclined her head.

pages.content:
The night before the championship final, {{NAME}} went to the park alone.

The unicorn was there, standing in the goal in the dark, her horn casting a soft silver light on the penalty spot.

He sat on the grass across from her and they stayed like that for a while, not practising, just being there.

"Thanks," he said finally.

She walked across the pitch and stood beside him, looking up at the stars.

He went home steady and calm, and slept a dreamless sleep, and in the morning he scored the winning penalty without thinking about it at all.
